chapter: Later life, World's Fair and Ellington
title: Working with Duke Ellington at the Rainbow Grill
summary: Hall subbed for bassist Joe Benjamin and describes Ellington's warmth.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Now, in this here last period of the '70s we talked -- you worked at La Chansonnette, you did the thing with Alberta Hunter and --
I worked with Duke Ellington in the '70s also.
Yeah, up at the Rainbow Grill?
At the Rainbow Grill.
With the small group?
Yes, uh-huh.
How did that come about?
Joe Benjamin, the bassist, had gotten in an auto accident.
Oh, the auto accident.
Twice -- so I did it twice.
He called you to do it?
Yeah, uh-huh.
Had you played with Duke before in your career, you know, just sitting in or --
No more than record. I made records.
Oh, you made the record with -- also with Johnny Hodges.
Yeah, Duke was on that.
Back to Back?
Back to Back and Side to Side.
"Side to Side." How was it to work with the band at the Rainbow Grill?
Oh, it was great, wonderful, yeah. And I can remember very vividly.
What qualities do you think made Ellington so unique other than the ones that are so obvious to us, you know. his talents as a composer, as a personality,
as a leader --
Well --
-- of knowing him as you did.

Well, the only thing I could add to that would be that he's just a warm human being. He's just a warm human being. He never was visibly riled or he didn't fire anybody in the band or -- except once -- Charlie Mingus.
(Laughter.)
Well, that's different.

But he -- whatever -- whatever he wrote, he wrote around the guys that played, their capabilities, and I think we played -- we played a 'Mood Indigo', and there were three horns at the mike. So he said, play it an octave higher, and way up on play it from the G string, which I did. And he says -- I wouldn't have asked you to do it if I didn't think you could do it.
(Laughter.)
He wanted that certain sound.
